title: Argentine Plains and Andine Glaciers
subtitle: Life on an Estancia, and an Expedition into the Andes
publisher: Charles Scribner’s Sons; T. Fisher Unwin
summary: Walter Larden, an Oxford lecturer and mountaineer, went out to Argentina in August 1908 to stay again on his brother’s estancia, Santa Isabel, in the province of Santa Fé, twenty years after his first stay there in 1888–9. The first part of the book describes the estancia then and now: the staff and the year’s work with cattle, sheep, and horses, the colonists, a locust invasion followed through its stages, and the birds, animals, insects, plants, and weather of the plains. The second part tells of an expedition in February and March 1909 by rail to Puente del Inca and on mules into the Andes, to the glaciers at the head of the Rio del Plomo and the Tupungato valley, with notes on penitentes, equipment, and mule-men. It ends with a visit to Chile and to an estancia in San Luis. Appendices give an account of the country with statistics, and a glossary of camp Spanish.
